To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
AC133 is an attractive target for CAR T cell therapy of GBM and that CD57 is upregulated on CAR T cells upon direct contact with GBM-SC.

AC133-specific CAR T cell therapy is a promising new treatment option for patients with glioblastoma, but that CD57 upregulation on the CAR T cell surface is an unspecific side-effect that may be caused by contact with GBM-SC-derived CD57+ cells.

the development of a novel AC133-CAR for immunotherapy of GBM and other AC133+ tumors, and the unexpected finding that CD57 may serve as a marker for activated T cells that are in contact with GBM cells.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

CD57 is not a CSC marker for GBMs but a potential marker for highly aggressive, undetermined, multipotent tumor cells of neural-crest origin, and it can be upregulated on T cells upon contact with these cells.
CD57 expression is a marker of T cell activation and differentiation in the context of GBM-SC therapy.
CD57 is not a marker for CSCs in GBM, but that CD57+ CSCs are present in GBM and can be killed by CD133-targeting CAR T cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GBM-SC killing by AC133-CAR-T cells is associated with the upregulation of the T cell aging and exhaustion marker CD57.
CD133-specific CAR-T cells kill GBM-SC in vitro and in vivo, but that GBM-SC induce the T cell marker CD57.
AC133-CART cells are able to kill AC133+ glioblastoma cells, but that the presence of CD57 on these cells is not indicative of their stem cell character.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CAR T cells may be useful for the treatment of GBM.
AC133-CART cells can kill patient-derived GBM CSCs in vitro and in vivo, but CD57 is not a CSC marker for GBMs.
CD57 is a useful marker for identifying activated human T cells, but it is not a useful marker for CSCs in GBM.
